sections.heading: EIP-8037/8038 Overview and Current Status
sections.summary: EIP-8037/8038 enable 3.3x gas scaling but break some smart contract invariants; outreach and audits slipped due to EF reorgs and budget cuts.
sections.body:
- Glamsterdam includes ePBS, Block Level Access Lists, and a scaling package (EIP-8037/8038) that raises the block gas limit from 60M to 200M gas.
- EIP-8037 and EIP-8038 were proposed in 2025 and will significantly reduce actual costs for most users despite some gas amounts increasing.
- Multiple contracts rely on invariants modified by 8037/8038; the EF's planned public outreach and audit timelines slipped due to EF reorganizations and budget cuts.
- Marius took personal responsibility as the last remaining scaling track lead still at the EF.
- ChainSecurity flagged the affected contracts, triggering internal investigation and broader mobilization.
- Marius noted that many AI-generated alternative proposals end up resembling a worse EOF spec, break other invariants, or primarily target invariants that aren't where most contracts actually break.
- [Vitalik's blog post](https://docs.fileverse.io/document/dUHG8ythBk3jJuQEjcE7m6#k=tVLgvLrIqyEsCh7qUmACb9ggVmybyS_aIZZsAMvHDAk) published same day covers upcoming invariant-breaking changes (e.g., all contracts relying on EC Recover will break with the PQ transition).
- Marius emphasized that modifying Glamsterdam could delay the roadmap by 4–6 months, impacting the PQ transition and Hegota.

sections.heading: ChainSecurity Audit Findings
sections.summary: ChainSecurity found 152 findings; most breakages stem from hard-coded gas budgets becoming insufficient, not from the new reservoir/refill mechanism.
sections.body:
- ChainSecurity was tasked by the EF with two objectives: find more protocols affected by 8037/8038, and find additional invariant breakages across Glamsterdam.
- Two search approaches used: AI agent swarm (starting from deployment lists, verified source code, on-chain activity) and trace-based replay of approximately one year of mainnet transactions.
- 152 findings identified, of which 76 overlapped with EF internal findings, bringing the combined total to ~200 findings.
  - Each "finding" represents a class of affected contracts, not a single contract address.
- Most findings relate to Invariants 4 and 7 (gas cost increases making hard-coded gas budgets insufficient), not the new reservoir or refill mechanism.
- Majority of findings can be mitigated relatively easily; a few require contract upgrades or full redeployment for immutable protocols.
- Additional risks found in Gloas (consensus-layer changes): proof layout changes can block staking operations; moving execution data can break indexers and oracles.
- ETH transfers to new accounts may fail at 21,000 gas due to new account creation costs.
- Coverage acknowledged as incomplete: dormant paths, unverified code, private off-chain systems, and L2s were not assessed.
- ChainSecurity drafted a guide on making try/catch patterns robust against future gas repricings; feedback requested via [glamsterdam-gas-invariants PR #4](https://github.com/ethereum/glamsterdam-gas-invariants/pull/4).
- [ChainSecurity slides](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1FyMPRzlsiOHzs4ia-3nAAaPGLmO_yzLurmvU2OIYI18/edit?usp=sharing) shared in chat.
- Discussion about whether the full report should be public or privately shared with affected protocols; Marius confirmed a big outreach campaign is underway to privately contact affected protocols.

sections.heading: Dedaub Audit Findings
sections.summary: Dedaub found 12 high and 70 medium confirmed findings from non-trivial gas patterns, plus additional findings from explicit non-default gas calls.
sections.body:
- Dedaub was contracted by the EF for an impact study on EIP-8037/8038.
- Two-pronged approach:
  - Part 1: Contracts with non-trivial GAS opcode patterns (any use of GAS opcode not intended to forward all remaining gas to an external call), filtered from decompiled contracts database, yielding ~25,000 contracts.
  - Part 2: Contracts passing explicit non-default gas to external calls, filtered by dynamic features (>100 transactions in a tight time frame or high-value recent transaction), also yielding ~25,000 contracts.
- Classification used static analysis, symbolic execution, AI triage, and manual inspection.
- Part 1 results: 12 high findings and 70 medium findings, all confirmed with EELS replays.
  - Only 22 contracts in the dataset were missed by Dedaub but found by EF internal search, giving confidence in coverage.
- Part 2 used source-level analysis patterns: conditionals on gas left, fixed reserves, fixed gas parameters.
  - Resulted in additional verified positives confirmed via transaction replays.
- Dedaub is currently coordinating with affected protocols on outreach, deduplicating with other teams' notifications.
- Neville (Dedaub) noted many findings will likely be "won't fix" and that the lack of a reliable mechanism for callers to distinguish OOG from logical revert is a broader UX issue, not specifically a Glamsterdam defect.
  - Suggested core devs consider an opcode to introspect last call status.

sections.heading: EF Internal Investigation and Application Outreach
sections.summary: EF found 3 high-severity cases (all being fixed) and at least 25 confirmed medium findings; 16 teams are actively triaging or have already patched.
sections.body:
- EF analysis replayed millions of transactions on L1 and used Sourcify to identify broken invariants.
- 3 high-severity findings: one already fixed, two plan to fix within the next month.
- At least 25 confirmed medium findings (actual number hidden due to high false-positive count).
  - 16 teams have acknowledged and are actively triaging or fixing; 3 have already fixed; 8 plan to fix by end of year.
  - Some teams contacted but not yet triaged.
- OP Stack: Optimism already fixed their invariants (live on OP Sepolia); coordination needed with independent OP Stack forks to replay on their testnets.
- ~89% of findings from hard-coded gas costs; the remainder involve 8037 reservoir/refill mechanics (per chat from spencer).
- Only 0.1% of transactions are affected (per Rahul in chat).
- Remaining immutable contracts with no upgrade path hold on the order of a few hundred thousand dollars in value.
- Marius noted the total affected contracts number is in the range of 10,000–15,000 out of ~90 million contracts on Ethereum.

sections.heading: Juicebox Protocol Concerns and Try/Catch Composability
sections.summary: Jango (Juicebox) warned that 8037 lets users tune gas to bypass composable try/catch blocks, undermining confidence in deploying immutable protocols.
sections.body:
- Jango explained Juicebox uses try/catch extensively for extensible pay and cash-out functions; under Glamsterdam, users can tune gas limits so composable extensions fail and trigger catch blocks, skipping intended logic.
- This effectively gives users implicit branching control over whether composability runs, which Jango described as a massive break to safe try/catch composability.
- Jango's PoCs shared at [mejango/glamsterdam-pocs](https://github.com/mejango/glamsterdam-pocs).
- Philosophical concern: invariant breakages for quantum/AI hardening are justifiable because they increase confidence, but 8037 may undermine developer confidence in building immutable protocols.
  - Asked whether it is now foolish to build immutable protocols on Ethereum, and if so, that should be stated clearly.
- Juicebox's direct financial exposure is ~$200K on the latest version, but the confidence impact is considered far more significant.
- Higher-level alternatives (pull payments, retry queues, gas pre-checks) all exist but are lossy or require new storage slots (110K gas under Glamsterdam) and second transactions.
- Daniel Gretzke (Uniswap) strongly echoed concerns, emphasizing that implicit branching based on user-set transaction gas fundamentally breaks contract development assumptions and creates second-order UX effects.
  - Said he would prefer to wait for increased contract size limits if it meant fixing 8037's other issues.
- Marius acknowledged the try/catch concern but noted most breakages are from hard-coded gas, which has been warned against for years; previous forks (EIP-2929/2930) already broke the absolute immutability assumption.
- Ben Adams noted in chat that moving refunds to end of transaction breaks ERC-4337 bundling, affecting current account abstraction.

sections.heading: Immutability, Invariant Documentation, and Future Guarantees
sections.summary: Consensus forming around creating formal documentation of which Ethereum invariants are guaranteed stable versus expected to change in future forks.
sections.body:
- Toni stressed the need to differentiate hard-coded gas breakages from invariant-level breakages (e.g., gas left being able to increase), and to formally define which properties are hard guarantees versus implementation specifics.
- Ansgar noted the distinction between guaranteed invariants (e.g., opcode behavior) and implementation specifics (e.g., gas prices, block header structure) is currently very fuzzy and must be made explicit.
  - SELFDESTRUCT cited as an important counterexample of opcode behavior changing.
- Marius supported creating documentation (possibly an EIP) listing invariants that will never change, invariants expected to change, and reasoning for each.
- Barnabas stated Ethereum cannot honestly promise true immutability given upcoming PQ, state repricing, and other necessary changes.
- Vitalik's blog post covers the "What about the future?" question directly, listing upcoming changes that will break existing contracts.
- Ansgar cautioned against rushing the invariant formalization work: "worst outcome would be to prematurely commit to something and then realize 3 months later that it wasn't quite right."
- Relevant community input: [pcaversaccio's take](https://github.com/ethereum/pm/issues/2299#issuecomment-6913931359) calls for formalizing invariants, incorporating them into specs, continuous testing, and testing deployed applications.

sections.heading: Improving Protocol-App Layer Alignment
sections.summary: EF created the Access Layer cluster with 3,000+ developer contacts; specs team adding deployed-contract invariant checks to the EIP testing process.
sections.body:
- The EF created the Access Layer cluster in the last year, with two teams: app enablement and builder enablement, focused on aligning the app layer with the protocol layer.
  - Builder enablement completed a survey with over 50 teams the EF doesn't usually coordinate with closely.
  - Through SEAL and other partnerships, they have access to ~3,000+ L1 developers and direct engineering/security contacts at major protocols.
- Rahul noted the Glamsterdam repricing outreach was a concrete use case for Access Layer resources; most contacted teams responded within one day.
- The decision to delay Glamsterdam was explicitly framed as putting apps first.
- For future hard forks, the EF plans talks at conferences on what invariants may break, months before the fork, not deferred to Devcon.
- Contact for app teams with repricing feedback: glamstdammit@ethereum.org.
- Specs team (Mario Vega) described new commitments:
  - Every specification change will now be evaluated through the app-layer lens.
  - When tests break, the team will stop and analyze why rather than auto-fixing.
  - New tooling PRs in development:
    - [ethereum/execution-specs#3948](https://github.com/ethereum/execution-specs/pull/3948): deployed-idiom invariant corpus.
    - [ethereum/execution-specs#3982](https://github.com/ethereum/execution-specs/pull/3982): check chain invariants while filling tests.
    - [ethereum/execution-specs#3905](https://github.com/ethereum/execution-specs/pull/3905): tool to run contracts against latest specs.
- ChainSecurity (Hubert) asked why the EF doesn't maintain in-house contract impact analysis capability; Marius explained the team was being built but lost to budget cuts and reorgs.
- Toni confirmed that AI-powered agent-based analysis (pioneered by Ethlabs/Francesco) will continue for future EIPs, and security audit firms should be engaged earlier.
- Multiple participants emphasized the need for the EF to use its public channels (e.g., 4M-follower Twitter account) for communicating fork impacts to the broader ecosystem.

sections.heading: Glamsterdam Path Forward and ACDE Decision
sections.summary: No decision made today; the ACDE call Thursday will determine whether Glamsterdam ships as-is, with strong sentiment to proceed but acknowledge the cost.
sections.body:
- Decision on whether to ship EIP-8037 explicitly deferred to the ACDE call on Thursday.
- Strong sentiment from core devs and researchers (Ansgar, Marius, Toni, spencer) to proceed with Glamsterdam as-is, primarily due to:
  - PQ transition urgency: Hegota depends on Glamsterdam (e.g., ePBS); splitting out a partial Glamsterdam would be very costly.
  - Spec changes to 8037 would introduce different broken invariants and wouldn't fix the ~90% of breakages from state cost increases.
  - Removing 8037 would also lose the ability to deploy max-size contracts (needed after EIP-7825 transaction limit cap).
- Ansgar stressed the cost of delaying: ~4 months pushed onto PQ account support, which needs the longest user migration runway.
- Marius noted affected protocols that have been contacted appear comfortable with a January Glamsterdam date.
- Spencer proposed agreeing on a Hoodi testnet fork date at the next ACDE to give a few days to absorb the information; Marius agreed.
- Jango and Daniel Gretzke pushed back, arguing 8037's reservoir mechanism specifically (not just gas cost increases) should be reconsidered and that sunk-cost fallacy should be avoided.
- Potuz noted even if 8037 ships, the timeline question matters: don't want to rush apps into upgrading on a tight schedule, but also don't want to be captured by non-upgrading apps.

sections.heading: Payload Binding Solution Selection
sections.summary: Deferred due to time constraints; to be discussed at a future call.
sections.body:
- jtraglia confirmed it was too late to discuss the payload binding topic (choosing between [consensus-specs PR #5770](https://github.com/ethereum/consensus-specs/pull/5770) and [PR #5820](https://github.com/ethereum/consensus-specs/pull/5820)).
- Will need to be rescheduled for a future call.

sections.heading: EIPIP Call: AI in the EIP Process
sections.summary: Jochem announced the EIPIP call Wednesday to discuss integrating AI into the EIP review process without degrading quality.
sections.body:
- Large influx of new EIPs and ERCs attributed to the AI boom.
- The EIPIP call on Wednesday November 18 at 16:00 UTC will discuss how to integrate AI into the review process while maintaining quality and trust.
- Agenda link: [ethereum/pm#2288](https://github.com/ethereum/pm/issues/2288).
- All interested parties invited to attend and contribute ideas.
